items.desc: Ecologists have long understood that biodiversity is paramount to ecosystem stability. items.desc: Scientists have uncovered new evidence that Venus may still be tearing itself apart from within. Advanced 3D simulations indicate that some of the planet's giant rift valleys formed relatively recently and could still be expanding. The results suggest Venus has a far more active interior than researchers once believed, challenging the long-held view of a geologically dormant world.

items.title: APOE2 may protect the brain from Alzheimer’s and aging
items.desc: The longevity-linked APOE2 gene appears to protect brain cells by reducing DNA damage and helping neurons recover from stress. The finding could open a new path toward treatments that mimic APOE2’s defenses in people at higher genetic risk for Alzheimer’s.

items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt challenges the story of human origins
items.desc: A newly identified fossil ape from northern Egypt is reshaping ideas about where the ancestors of modern apes first emerged. Analyses place it closer to living apes than any known East African species of the same age, pointing to North Africa and the Middle East as a possible birthplace and crossroads for the ape lineage that eventually produced gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and humans.

items.title: Sweden’s hidden rare earth deposits could help break China’s grip
items.desc: Sweden could become an important source of rare earth elements needed for magnets and green technologies. Instead of extracting one target metal, researchers are cataloging everything contained in Swedish mineral deposits. They will then develop magnets using those naturally available combinations, potentially reducing pollution, waste, and reliance on China.

items.title: China’s Tianwen-1 captures interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS near Mars
items.desc: China’s Tianwen-1 orbiter captured a faint but remarkable view of 3I/ATLAS as the interstellar comet raced past Mars. The images reveal its tail and glowing coma, offering scientists a glimpse of material born beyond our solar system.

items.title: Scientists discover the Sun contains 55% more silver than expected
items.desc: A new analysis suggests the Sun holds far more silver than earlier estimates indicated. More advanced models of the solar atmosphere raised the calculated amount by 55 percent, bringing it into much closer agreement with ancient meteorites. The technique may also help scientists track the cosmic origins of silver and other heavy elements.

items.title: Orcas filmed smashing giant sunfish into thousands of pieces
items.desc: Researchers in the Gulf of California have documented a dramatic orca behavior never described before. In two separate encounters, one orca gripped a dead sunfish by the fin while another charged into it at high speed, blasting the carcass into thousands of pieces.

items.title: A strange quantum effect dramatically boosts energy transfer
items.desc: Researchers discovered a proton-assisted mechanism that greatly improves how triplet energy moves between quantum dots and nearby molecules. The proton briefly shifts position, helps coordinate electron movement, and then returns to where it started. This quantum-driven shuttle could offer a powerful new way to tune solar cells, lasers, and catalytic reactions.

items.title: New giant salamander species discovered in 3.5-million-year-old fossils
items.desc: Fossils discovered in Japan more than two decades ago have finally been identified as a new genus and species of giant salamander. Limnospondylus ajimuensis lived around 3.5 million years ago in a warmer, wetter Kyushu and may have reached 1.1 meters in length. Its discovery hints that many more unknown giant salamanders could be hiding among fossils previously given the wrong classification.

items.title: Scientists discover the hidden brain switch that assigns bees their jobs
items.desc: Researchers found that specific brain circuits help decide which jobs bees perform as they age. When those circuits were switched off, older worker bees began caring for the queen again instead of carrying out their normal later-life duties. The findings reveal that a bee colony’s complex division of labor may be guided by neural switches hidden inside each bee’s brain.

items.title: NASA will test SpaceX and Blue Origin Moon landers before the next lunar landing
items.desc: NASA is preparing for future astronaut landings on the Moon with an unusually ambitious orbital rehearsal. During Artemis III in 2027, Orion astronauts will rendezvous and dock separately with prototype lunar landers from Blue Origin and SpaceX, allowing crews and ground teams to test the complex maneuvers needed for later missions.

items.title: NASA’s Webb telescope discovers giant planet hiding in one of astronomy’s most famous systems
items.desc: A giant planet had been hiding inside one of astronomy’s most closely studied planetary systems, concealed by a bright disk of cosmic dust. Webb revealed Beta Pictoris d through atmospheric traces of carbon monoxide, water vapor, and methane, showcasing a promising new method for finding elusive exoplanets.

items.title: How Burnham Can Make UK Devolution Work
items.desc: Andy Burnham’s first 100 days as prime minister of the United Kingdom will need to be devoted to building the institutional architecture for his vision of devolved governance to succeed. The question is not where to concentrate decision-making authority, but how to ensure that different authorities are working together.

items.title: West Africa Needs Its Own Draghi Moment
items.desc: Senegal’s debt crisis has exposed a deeper vulnerability within West Africa’s monetary union. Unable to devalue the shared currency, member countries must either endure painful internal adjustment or boost exports to earn the foreign currency they need to repay external creditors.

items.title: Will the Real Marco Rubio Please Stand Up?
items.desc: Is US Secretary of State Marco Rubio an embattled champion of Venezuelan democracy within the Trump administration, or the public face of a strategy aimed at keeping the old regime in power? Six months after Nicolás Maduro’s ouster, his record suggests democratic restoration is no longer an American priority—if it ever was.

items.title: How AI Could Reinforce Dollar Dominance
items.desc: While policymakers and economists debate the future of dollar dominance, AI companies, cloud providers, and payment networks might already be writing it into the next chapter of international monetary history. Those who hope to shape that chapter must act now—or risk being left off the page.

items.title: What Ukraine’s Success Means for the West
items.desc: There are several reasons why Ukraine has been able to stymie its much larger aggressor. For the world’s democracies, the most important lesson to draw from Ukrainians' doggedness and brilliant innovations and improvisations may be that we should not be so surprised.

items.title: The Strong Suffer What They Must
items.desc: Foolish military interventions driven by outdated calculations of economic power have thoroughly discredited the old big powers. Thucydides might well have appreciated the irony of a world in which smaller, weaker countries like Ukraine and Iran can expose Russia and the United States, respectively, as paper tigers.

items.title: Why Iran Won’t Change

This helps to explain why the US and Israel were wrong to expect the regime to change its behavior, let alone be brought down by the Iranian people.

items.title: Rethinking Global Imbalances
items.desc: Today’s global imbalances, starting with China's massive trade surplus, are not simply the result of poor macroeconomic coordination. Rather, they reflect long-term strategic thinking and a departure from the bias toward openness on which the postwar trade order was built.

items.title: What the New UK Chancellor Means for the UK Economy

If Healey can leverage his insider knowledge of the Treasury, pursue a bold, pro-growth agenda, and manage his defense-spending instincts, he may be able to provide the structural shake-up the UK economy needs.
